overview: Turcik tribes is the atlas's exact spelling, but no reviewed source identifies one people by that name between 200 and 100 BCE. The spelling itself likely reflects a modern error in transmission. The sole polygon stretches almost sixty degrees of longitude, from the western Siberian forest-steppe through Altai, Minusinsk, Tuva, Baikal, and Transbaikal. It excludes Mongolia and southern Kazakhstan, so it is not a credible state, frontier, speech map, or ethnic census. Archaeology instead reveals different local settings: Sargat settlements and graves in the west, changing Tagar and Tes traditions around Minusinsk, Tuva cemeteries, Baikal fisher-forager evidence, and Xiongnu-period farms and workshops near Ivolga in the east. Houses, woven belts, spindle whorls, crops, herds, fish, teeth, parasites, and burials illuminate work and family life, but none labels its makers Turkic. The dates below are teaching slices across broad evidence ranges, not invented decade-by-decade events. No securely attributable local written-language sample survives for this umbrella and interval. At 100 BCE the map erases the id, while communities, languages, technologies, and exchange continued along many separate paths.

periods.title: 200 to 188 BCE: one atlas umbrella appears
periods.summary: The exact id appears only in the 200 BCE snapshot. Western Sargat, Minusinsk Tagar or Tes, Tuva, Baikal, and Transbaikal evidence overlaps the broad window, but no archaeological event united the entire polygon in 200 BCE. This first slice records software coverage, not a founding.

periods.title: 188 to 176 BCE: western forest-steppe life continues
periods.summary: Radiocarbon evidence places active Sargat use of western Siberian forest-steppe sites across centuries including this slice. The sample is uneven and dominated by the Tobol region, so it cannot support a precise western border, a single population, or a dated political change during these twelve years.

periods.title: 176 to 164 BCE
periods.summary: Minusinsk radiocarbon results place the Tes phase from the second century BCE into later centuries, while artifact chronologies differ. This slice marks overlap within a debated sequence and does not identify an ethnicity, language, or abrupt replacement during this span.

periods.title: 164 to 152 BCE: food evidence complicates nomad stereotypes
periods.summary: Dental and isotope work at Ai-Dai and Aymyrlyg finds cereals, especially millet, plus fish alongside animal products. The cemeteries have broad Early Iron Age ranges, so their evidence supports regional economic variety, not an exact menu for this twelve-year slice or every household inside the polygon.

periods.title: 152 to 140 BCE: Ivolga joins an eastern settlement story
periods.summary: Ivolga's settlement sequence extends from the late third century BCE into the first century CE. Houses, storage pits, crops, fish, wild fauna, and domestic animals show settled production within a wider Xiongnu-period landscape. They do not make the western half of this polygon Xiongnu.

periods.title: 140 to 128 BCE: neighbors share drawn seams
periods.summary: At the 200 BCE snapshot, the target shares encoded arcs with Xiongnu, Yuezhi, Scythian, Tungus, and Paleo-Siberian features. Those seams explain the atlas mosaic, not five guarded frontiers. The evidence inside each neighboring label has its own chronology, scale, and uncertainties.

periods.title: 128 to 116 BCE: parasites preserve one difficult meal story
periods.summary: Soil from second-century BCE onward burials at Tunnug 1 contains parasite eggs consistent with freshwater fish and animal-food exposure. This remarkable trace supports varied foodways and health risks in Tuva. It does not identify a shared recipe, diagnosis, or sanitation rule across northern Eurasia.

periods.title: 116 to 100 BCE: the card ends, communities do not
periods.summary: The exact id is absent from the 100 BCE map, which reallocates its enormous space among other atlas features. No reviewed archaeological source reports a matching continent-wide collapse, migration, or language switch. This final slice ends a database interval while local histories remain continuous and diverse.

sections.title: Decode the label and the enormous polygon

items.text: The exact index entry reads Turcik tribes, a circa culture dated 200 to 100 BCE and generated from historical basemaps. Coverage finds one border file and no existing card. Turcik is therefore preserved as an imported spelling to explain, not silently promoted into an ancient self-name.

Only world-bc200 contains the id. Its decoded Polygon has one ring, 20 positions, and bounds from about 64.74 to 124.13 degrees east and 48.31 to 59.82 degrees north. That clean outline is an editorial object, not an excavated fence or a remembered political boundary.

Point tests place Petropavl, Omsk, Novosibirsk, Barnaul, Altai, Minusinsk, Tuva, Irkutsk, northern Baikal, Buryatia, and Chita inside. Astana, the Urals, Tarim, Dzungaria, Ulaanbaatar, Ordos, Manchuria, and Yakutsk fall outside. The selection fits no simple ethnic or linguistic homeland or polity.

The polygon directly shares TopoJSON arcs with atlas regions labeled Paleo-Siberian hunter-gatherers, Xiongnu, Yuezhi, Scythians, and Tungus. These are file-construction seams. They cannot prove treaties, guarded checkpoints, exclusive territories, or that the people on either side accepted the atlas's modern categories.

The id is absent at 323 and 300 BCE, appears at 200 BCE, and vanishes at 100 BCE. Between 100 and 1 BCE, owners around Irkutsk, Buryatia, and Chita change again. These software seams are suspiciously abrupt; human households and languages did not repaint themselves on schedule.

sections.title: Ask what the evidence can really identify

items.text: Western Siberian archaeology uses material-culture names such as Sargat for recurring site patterns, not recovered passports. Radiocarbon research draws on 118 contexts from seven settlements and fifteen mound cemeteries, yet sampling is uneven and Tobol-heavy. A large sample can still have a lopsided map.

Minusinsk researchers divide Tagar evidence into phases using burial construction, ceremony, artifacts, and radiocarbon dates. Tes ranges vary by method, reaching from the second century BCE into later centuries. A phase name organizes evidence; it does not automatically identify a language, tribe, or biological population.

Tagar scholarship has long favored spectacular graves, while settlements and houses remain much less understood. A Liverpool study warns that dwelling classification still needs improvement. This imbalance makes ordinary life harder to see and cautions against letting rich tombs speak for every cook, herder, or builder.

A 2026 series of 168 radiocarbon dates finds varied Tes and Tashtyk mortuary practices and later coexistence rather than a crisp replacement. Most modeled overlap lies after this card, but the result matters here: archaeological labels can change gradually, and older period boundaries deserve testing.

The earliest people securely called Turk in historical scholarship appear in the sixth century CE, centuries after this card. Earlier communities certainly had languages and names, but pots, graves, genes, and horse gear cannot supply them. Calling the whole polygon Proto-Turkic would overstate a disputed reconstruction.

sections.title: Build homes and make daily meals

items.text: Sargat builders used at least five dwelling forms, including light cone-shaped structures, frame-and-pillar buildings, timber wall techniques, and insulated houses. Several chambers with different functions could join into one homestead complex. Western forest-steppe domestic life was architecturally varied, not a row of identical tents.

Some Sargat rooms were sunk into the ground, while builders mixed timber techniques and used topsoil for insulation. Long passages and connected chambers structured movement through a homestead. Archaeology sees walls and floors better than sleeping places, recipes, privacy rules, or who complained about drafts.

At Ivolga, archaeologists recorded pit and surface houses, fireplaces, chimneys, storage pits, and a thick occupation layer. Cultivated wheat, rye, and barley occurred beside fish and wild and domestic animals. This eastern settlement economy was mixed, settled, and productive within a broader mobile landscape.

Three newly investigated Ivolga dwellings ended differently: one pit was filled during occupation with pottery, household objects, and animal bones, while two structures were abandoned and burned. Those deposits reveal sequences of use and loss. They do not explain every fire or identify each resident.

Ai-Dai and Aymyrlyg teeth and bone chemistry indicate cereals, especially millet, fish, and animal products. The balance varied between studied populations and individuals. Meals were therefore more flexible than an all-meat nomad stereotype, though cemetery samples cannot reconstruct each season, cooking pot, or child's appetite.

sections.title: Move with animals and riding technology

items.text: Earlier Altai riders used saddles made from two leather cushions beneath decorated saddle cloths. Pazyryk preservation predates this card, so it supplies regional background rather than a universal second-century BCE kit. A saddle documents skilled leather, textile, and horse work; it does not reveal the rider's language.

Xiongnu-period settlement surveys east of the atlas polygon distinguish large riverside sites from smaller tributary sites and suggest seasonal movement. Ivolga adds a major permanent settlement. Mobility and houses could coexist within regional systems, so settled does not mean immobile and herder does not mean homeless.

At Aymyrlyg, skeletal trauma has been studied alongside environment, occupations, and warfare. Injuries can reflect riding, work, accidents, or violence, and context matters. The research offers a population-level window into demanding lives, not a license to turn every healed bone into a cavalry adventure.

Ivolga's animal remains include cattle, sheep, goats, horses, pigs, dogs, and other domestic taxa, alongside hunted animals and fish. This diversity shows that stock keeping sat within a wider food and work system. Species lists alone cannot reconstruct herd ownership, seasonal routes, or favorite animals.

Dietary isotopes from Minusinsk and Tuva show that pastoral economies incorporated crops and fish. Herding was important without being exclusive. Families could move animals, cultivate or obtain grain, and use rivers in different combinations, which is far more useful than squeezing every northern community into one economic costume.

Chepkul-9 preserved woven Sargat belts made from wool and plant fibers, dated broadly from the third century BCE to first century CE. Scientific textile analysis reconstructed how they were made. A belt held clothing and displayed skill, though a burial belt may not represent everyone's everyday wardrobe.

Most Sargat mounds were looted, so surviving belt fragments are unusually valuable. Researchers combine plan, stratigraphy, fiber analysis, and comparison with other burials. Even a narrow strip of cloth can preserve choices about spinning, weaving, color, fit, and presentation that metal-heavy grave inventories miss.

Ceramic spindle whorls from Galechnoye-1 are direct tools of textile production at a Sargat settlement in the Baraba forest-steppe. They show spinning as practiced work outside elite tomb display. The whorls do not identify who spun, whether children helped, or which fiber entered every thread.

Ivolga houses yielded pottery and household objects within lived and abandoned deposits. Their study connects craft products with rooms, storage, fires, and animal remains instead of treating artifacts as floating art. A broken pot may be ordinary rubbish, a chronological clue, and evidence of skilled making all at once.

Eastern steppe archaeology identifies industrial production and long-range exchange within the Xiongnu political world, alongside local settlements and herding. These networks could move objects and techniques across communities. Shared goods demonstrate contact, but they do not make Sargat, Tagar, Tuva, and Transbaikal residents one ethnic group.

sections.title: Keep family and social life evidence-sized

items.text: Sargat burial researchers analyze bodies and accompanying objects as one assemblage to propose gender patterns. They explicitly frame results as hypotheses. Graves show that age, sex, status, and ritual treatment mattered, but they cannot directly reproduce marriages, residence rules, inheritance, affection, or arguments within living households.

Sargat women could receive woven belts and varied grave goods, while gendered burial patterns differed among cemeteries. Objects associated with one burial do not define every woman's occupation or authority. Social roles were structured and locally variable, and mortuary presentation could simplify a much messier life.

Children appear in Sargat cemeteries with sharply different treatment, including a richly furnished child in a unique boat burial and other children with few goods. That variation shows children had social identities. It does not prove a universal age ladder or that grave wealth equaled daily comfort.

Non-metric dental traits from 480 buried people reveal that Sargat groups in the Tobol, Ishim, Irtysh, and Baraba areas were not biologically interchangeable. Baraba shows stronger local continuity than several western groups. Teeth can trace population relationships, but neither ancestry nor anatomy speaks a language.

Ivolga's houses, storage facilities, crafts, and cemetery imply people of many ages living within a fortified settlement, but room plans do not map neatly onto nuclear families. A household might include kin, dependents, workers, guests, or captives. The evidence supports community organization without recovering everyone's relationship.

sections.title: Let children learn without inventing schools

items.text: DNA from nine people in two Baraba Sargat mounds found some close paternal and maternal relationships but no parent-child pair. This tiny cemetery sample shows that graves can group relatives without representing whole households. It cannot reconstruct how children learned, who cared for them, or where they slept.

Spinning with a weighted spindle requires practiced control, while complex timber houses require measuring, joining, insulating, and repair. Younger people probably learned through watching and participation. That is a cautious skill-based inference, not evidence for a named teacher, classroom, written lesson, or universal training age.

Herding, riding, fishing, crop processing, and food storage likewise depended on repeated learning. Archaeology identifies tools, animals, foods, and spaces more readily than lessons. Children may have joined work gradually, but the surviving evidence cannot assign the same chores or freedoms across western forest-steppe and Transbaikal households.

Different dwelling types and multi-chamber homesteads would have shaped where people worked and watched one another. Children could learn social expectations through shared space, but archaeology cannot hear correction, praise, jokes, songs, or stories. A floor plan is useful evidence and a very poor school transcript.

No exact-period school, alphabet lesson, or child's writing is securely attributable to this atlas umbrella. The first certainly Turkic texts belong many centuries later. Spoken teaching certainly existed in unknown languages, but printing a reconstructed Proto-Turkic word here would turn a modern linguistic hypothesis into fake homework.

sections.title: Read teeth, bones, and parasites as health clues

items.text: Minusinsk dental research records caries, calculus, enamel hypoplasia, tooth wear, and age-related deterioration across long archaeological sequences. Tagar patterns may reflect greater cereal use, but teeth preserve outcomes rather than diagnoses. They cannot tell which pain remedy, healer, or caregiving routine an individual received.

At Ai-Dai and Aymyrlyg, dental lesions and stable isotopes are interpreted together because either line alone can mislead. Cereal and fish signals complicate a meat-only picture. The studies reconstruct population diets, not a medical chart, and they leave many illnesses that never marked bone invisible.

Tunnug 1 soil preserved eggs from whipworm, tapeworm-like parasites, and fish tapeworm. Freshwater fish was definitely eaten and may sometimes have been raw or undercooked. Infection documents bodily cost within a flexible pastoral diet, not ignorance, a moral failing, or one universal cooking habit.

Aymyrlyg skeletons preserve healed and unhealed trauma connected with accidents, work, riding, conflict, and possibly surgery. Context and lesion pattern matter more than heroic storytelling. Survival after injury can imply care, but the record rarely identifies who provided it, which treatment worked, or how pain was managed.

Cis-Baikal researchers compare paired human and terrestrial-animal radiocarbon dates with nitrogen isotopes because fish consumption can make human dates appear older. The method improves chronology and reveals diet at once. It also warns that a precise laboratory number may hide what someone ate, a surprisingly personal complication.

sections.title: Follow water, waste, sanitation, and absent toilets

items.text: Ivolga stood near the Selenga in a mosaic of steppe, forest, and river environments. Fish remains and crops show that water supported food and settlement. The evidence does not identify drinking wells, boiling routines, washing rules, or water ownership, so those household details must remain open.

Rivers and freshwater food also complicate radiocarbon dating around Baikal. People who ate much fish could carry older carbon into their bones, shifting apparent dates. That is excellent evidence for dietary water connections, but it says nothing direct about whether drinking water was clean, shared, stored, or filtered.

Parasite eggs at Tunnug reveal exposure pathways through fish and animals, while burial soil provides the testing context. They do not by themselves locate a latrine or prove that waste polluted a particular water source. Archaeoparasitology can expose risk without reconstructing an entire sanitation system.

Ivolga dwelling fill contained pottery, household debris, and animal bones, showing that waste entered abandoned or infilled spaces. Depositional history matters because rubbish can move after use. The finds do not establish where residents normally discarded refuse, dung, wastewater, or human waste while the houses remained occupied.

No reviewed exact-period source identifies a sewer or purpose-built toilet for the enormous atlas polygon. That silence is not proof that people ignored privacy or cleanliness. Latrines can be archaeologically shy when pits, screens, ash, soil, and organic matter are reused, eroded, or never excavated.

sections.title: Handle language, writing, achievement, and continuity

items.text: The imported word Turcik is best treated as a modern misspelling or malformed label, not an ancient ethnonym. Cambridge history places the securely traceable name Turk in the sixth century CE. Correcting the spelling to Turkic would still not prove who spoke what across this second-century BCE polygon.

Written-language sample: none securely attributable to the exact people and window. The first people to whom scholars can certainly assign a Turkic text are the later Turks, and their name is not securely traceable before the sixth century CE. A later inscription would be a mislabeled time traveler here.

Speech in these communities was real but undocumented. Archaeological cultures, burial phases, and genetic relationships cannot be read aloud. Proto-Turkic is a comparative linguistic reconstruction, not a script found at Ivolga, Minusinsk, or a Sargat settlement, so this card prints no reconstructed word as ancient writing.

Achievements visible in the evidence include varied insulated houses, multi-room homesteads, spinning and woven belts, mixed farming and herding, riding equipment, fishing, storage, settlement construction, and long-distance exchange. These were cumulative accomplishments of many local communities, not inventions of one imagined Turcik nation.

At 100 BCE the exact id disappears, but Sargat sites, Minusinsk traditions, Tuva communities, Baikal lifeways, and Xiongnu-period settlements continue on their own chronologies. The ending is atlas continuity, not conquest or extinction. The most honest legacy is plural: skills, people, and connections changed without one shared finale.

ending.text: The 100 BCE endpoint is a map and database seam. The exact id disappears and its vast footprint is redistributed among other atlas labels, without a matching continent-wide destruction layer, migration, or language change. Western forest-steppe, Minusinsk, Tuva, Baikal, and Transbaikal communities continued through distinct local histories. No single people ended because this umbrella did.
